newsitem.title: USA: Emerging market capital flows to decline this year.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market capital flows to decline this year.

text.p: The Institute of International Finance on Tuesday projected that net private flows to leading emerging markets will fall to $249 billion this year compared with $255 billion in 1996.

The financial institution group said that equity flows to some 29 leading emerging market economies are expected to reach $117 billion this year, after amounting to $113 billion in 1996, and now account for more than 45 percent of total flows.
The institute said there were fewer than 30 emerging market equity funds in industrial countries a decade ago, and now there are almost 1,500.

The institute said that although private capital flows remain somewhat concentrated, 31 countries have tapped global capital markets for the first time in the past two years, raising the total of countries with market access from 25 to 56.

In a briefing for reporters, IIF managing director Charles Dallara said that industrial governments, emerging market economies, multilateral institutions and others must work to sustain net private capital flows.
"Not withstanding the positive trends evident, there are some posssible risks to sustaining private capital flows at this time," he said.
These include uneven industrial country performance, a slackening of reforms in emerging market economies, diminished influence of multilateral institutions and "some injudicious lending."

He noted, for example, that spreads on emerging market bonds narrowed greatly in 1996 and early 1997 and while there was some widening in March, in most cases, they remain well below the levels of a year ago.
"This raises questions about whether spreads in all cases adequately reflect risks," he said.

The institute also issued a letter to the International Monetary Fund's interim committee saying in part that sound, coordinated policies are essential for a healthy world economy and growing exports for emerging market economies.

The letter sent in conjunction with the semi-annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank, which begins this week, said that sustained higher growth in Europe will require not only careful management of further fiscal consolidation with sound monetary policy, but policies to liberalize market structures.

It said Japan should implement its program of deregulation while confronting the weakness of its financial sector. It also said the United States must cope with the apparent strength of its economy without allowing inflationary pressures to rise or the expansion to be stifled.
